questions.keyword: Leases under ASC 842 — lessor classification criteria (operating vs. sales-type/direct financing), lessor journal entries, sale-leaseback accounting, lessee right-of-use asset and lease liability recognition and measurement
questions.text: Under ASC 842, a lessor must classify each lease as either an operating lease, a sales-type lease, or a direct financing lease. Which criterion, if met, results in a SALES-TYPE lease classification?

answers.text: The lease term is the major part of the underlying asset's remaining economic life (using 75% as a practical expedient), OR the present value of the lease payments and residual value guaranteed by the lessee equals substantially all of the fair value of the underlying asset (using 90% as a practical expedient)
The lease term is less than one year — short-term leases are always sales-type
The lessor retains title to the asset throughout the lease and has a remarketing agreement with the lessee
The lease contains variable lease payments tied to the performance of the leased asset — performance-linked payments always create sales-type treatment

explanations.a: Under ASC 842-10-25-2 (using the practical expedients from legacy ASC 840 bright-line tests), a sales-type lease exists when any ONE of these criteria is met: (1) the lease transfers ownership of the underlying asset; (2) the lease contains a purchase option that the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise; (3) the lease term is the major part of the remaining economic life of the underlying asset (75% practical expedient); (4) the present value of lease payments plus any residual value guaranteed by the lessee equals or exceeds substantially all of the asset's fair value (90% practical expedient); (5) the underlying asset is of such a specialized nature that the expected residual value is zero only to the lessor. If any single criterion is met → sales-type lease. The lessor recognizes a net investment (receivable) and derecognizes the leased asset, recognizing a selling profit/loss.
explanations.b: Short-term leases (12 months or less) qualify for the short-term lease exemption from ASC 842 recognition requirements — they are not classified as sales-type leases. Short-term leases allow lessors to continue recognizing income on a straight-line basis without complex lease accounting.
explanations.c: Retaining title does NOT create sales-type treatment — in a sales-type lease, the economic benefits are substantially transferred even if legal title is retained. Remarketing agreements relate to residual value risk management, not lease classification. Operating leases typically involve the lessor retaining the asset and its residual risks.
explanations.d: Variable lease payments tied to performance (e.g., based on sales volume) are excluded from the measurement of lease payments for classification purposes. The presence of variable payments does not determine the type of classification — the five classification criteria listed in option B govern the determination.

questions.name: Technical Accounting and Reporting
questions.keyword: Leases under ASC 842 — lessor classification criteria (operating vs. sales-type/direct financing), lessor journal entries, sale-leaseback accounting, lessee right-of-use asset and lease liability recognition and measurement
questions.text: A lessee enters into a 5-year operating lease for office space with annual lease payments of $120,000. The lessee's incremental borrowing rate is 6%. The PV annuity factor for 5 years at 6% is 4.212. Prepare the initial recognition journal entry and the Year 1 lease expense and payment entries.

answers.text: No journal entry at inception — operating leases are not recognized on the balance sheet under ASC 842
Inception: Dr. Right-of-Use (ROU) Asset $505,440 / Cr. Lease Liability $505,440; Year 1: Dr. Lease Expense $120,000 / Cr. Cash $120,000 (straight-line expense)
Inception: Dr. ROU Asset $600,000 / Cr. Lease Liability $600,000 (undiscounted payments); Year 1: Dr. Lease Expense $120,000 / Cr. Cash $120,000
Inception: Dr. ROU Asset $505,440 / Cr. Lease Liability $505,440; Year 1: Dr. Interest Expense $30,326 / Dr. Amortization Expense $89,674 / Cr. Cash $120,000 (finance lease treatment)

explanations.a: ASC 842 requires ALL leases with a term greater than 12 months (except short-term leases using the practical expedient) to be recognized on the balance sheet with a right-of-use asset and lease liability. This was one of the most significant changes from ASC 840, which kept operating leases off-balance-sheet.
explanations.b: Operating lease inception and Year 1 accounting: Inception: PV of lease payments = $120,000 × 4.212 = $505,440. Dr. Right-of-Use Asset $505,440 / Cr. Lease Liability $505,440. Both the ROU asset and lease liability are initially measured at the present value of remaining lease payments, discounted at the lessee's incremental borrowing rate (or the rate implicit in the lease if determinable). Year 1 accounting: Operating lease expense = Annual payment × straight-line allocation = $120,000 per year (single-line lease cost under the operating lease model). Dr. Lease Expense $120,000 / Cr. Cash $120,000. The ROU asset and lease liability amortize through the lease expense — the lease liability reduces by the difference between the cash payment and the interest component, while the ROU asset reduces by the difference needed to keep the total lease expense straight-line. No separate interest or amortization is shown for operating leases (unlike finance leases).
explanations.c: Using undiscounted cash flows ($600,000 = $120,000 × 5) instead of PV overstates both the ROU asset and lease liability. ASC 842 requires present value measurement.
explanations.d: This journal entry structure (separate interest and amortization) describes FINANCE LEASE accounting, not operating lease accounting. Operating leases use a single straight-line lease expense with no separate interest recognition.

questions.name: Technical Accounting and Reporting
questions.keyword: Leases under ASC 842 — lessor classification criteria (operating vs. sales-type/direct financing), lessor journal entries, sale-leaseback accounting, lessee right-of-use asset and lease liability recognition and measurement
questions.text: A manufacturer sells a building (carrying amount $2,000,000, FMV $3,000,000) to a real estate company for $3,000,000 cash and immediately leases it back under a 10-year operating lease (annual rent $200,000). The transaction qualifies as a sale under ASC 606. Prepare the seller-lessee's journal entry at the transaction date, including the gain recognition.

answers.text: Dr. Cash $3,000,000 / Cr. Building $2,000,000 / Cr. Gain on Sale $1,000,000; no lease entries needed at closing
The entire $3,000,000 proceeds are recognized as a financing liability — sale-leaseback transactions are always treated as financing arrangements
Dr. Cash $3,000,000 / Dr. ROU Asset (PV of lease payments) / Cr. Building $2,000,000 / Cr. Lease Liability (PV of lease payments) / Cr. Gain on Sale $1,000,000
Dr. Cash $3,000,000 / Cr. Building $2,000,000 / Cr. Deferred Gain $1,000,000; gain is amortized over the lease term

explanations.a: When the transaction qualifies as a sale, the lessee must also recognize the leaseback — a right-of-use asset and lease liability arise for the operating lease portion. Simply recording the sale proceeds without recognizing the leaseback obligation would omit the new lease from the balance sheet.
explanations.b: If the transfer does NOT qualify as a sale under ASC 606 (e.g., the seller retains a repurchase right, the lease payments are off-market in a way suggesting financing), then the transaction is treated as a financing arrangement — the asset stays on the seller's books and the proceeds are recorded as a liability. But the question states the transaction QUALIFIES as a sale, so financing treatment does not apply.
explanations.c: Sale-leaseback accounting under ASC 842 (when transfer is a sale): Seller-lessee entry at transaction date: (1) Derecognize the building: remove at carrying amount; (2) Recognize cash proceeds: $3,000,000 cash received; (3) Recognize ROU asset and lease liability for the leaseback: ROU asset = PV of lease payments (using incremental borrowing rate); (4) Recognize gain: gain = sale price ($3,000,000) minus carrying amount ($2,000,000) = $1,000,000 — this gain is recognized IMMEDIATELY (not deferred) under ASC 842. Journal entry: Dr. Cash $3,000,000; Dr. ROU Asset (PV of $200,000 × annuity factor); Cr. Building $2,000,000; Cr. Lease Liability (PV of lease payments); Cr. Gain on Sale $1,000,000. Note: This is a change from prior GAAP (ASC 840), which deferred and amortized gains on sale-leaseback transactions. Under ASC 842, if it's a true sale, the gain is immediate.
explanations.d: Deferred gain amortization over the lease term was the treatment under ASC 840 (old GAAP). ASC 842 eliminated deferred gain treatment for qualifying sale-leaseback transactions — the gain is recognized immediately when the transfer qualifies as a sale under ASC 606.

questions.name: Technical Accounting and Reporting
questions.keyword: Leases under ASC 842 — lessor classification criteria (operating vs. sales-type/direct financing), lessor journal entries, sale-leaseback accounting, lessee right-of-use asset and lease liability recognition and measurement
questions.text: A lessor enters into a lease for specialized manufacturing equipment (cost $500,000, useful life 8 years). The lease term is 7 years with annual payments of $90,000. The implicit rate is 5%. The present value of lease payments at 5% for 7 years is $520,782. The asset has no residual value at the end of the lease. Determine the lessor's lease classification and explain the Day 1 journal entry.

answers.text: Operating lease — the lease term (7 years) is not the major part of the asset's 8-year life because 7/8 = 87.5%, which is close to but does not meet the 75% bright-line test
Operating lease — specialized assets are always classified as operating leases because the lessor retains all risks of the specialized equipment
Direct financing lease — the asset has no residual value and the PV of payments exceeds cost, so it must be a direct financing lease

Sales-type lease — the PV of lease payments ($520,782) exceeds the asset's fair value ($500,000), indicating substantially all risks and rewards transfer; additionally, the 7/8 = 87.5% exceeds the 75% major part threshold; lessor records net investment and derecognizes the asset, recognizing $20,782 profit on Day 1

explanations.a: 87.5% (7 years out of 8-year life) substantially exceeds the 75% major part threshold. When this criterion is met, the lease is classified as sales-type, not operating.
explanations.b: Specialized assets do not automatically classify as operating leases. In fact, ASC 842 identifies a specialized nature asset (with no alternative use and no expected residual value at end of lease) as one of the criteria for sales-type classification. The specialized nature here (no residual value) further supports sales-type, not operating, classification.
explanations.c: Direct financing leases arise when the lease would have been classified as sales-type EXCEPT that the seller-dealer profit (or loss) at lease commencement is zero — the fair value equals cost. Here, $520,782 (PV of payments) > $500,000 (cost) → there IS a selling profit of $20,782 → this is a sales-type lease, not direct financing. Direct financing applies when the PV of payments equals the asset's cost (zero profit), which can occur when the lessor is a financial institution, not a manufacturer or dealer.
explanations.d: Lease classification analysis: Criterion check — lease term 7/8 years = 87.5% > 75% major part → SALES-TYPE criterion met. Also, PV of payments ($520,782) > fair value of asset ($500,000) → 104% exceeds 90% substantially all threshold → second sales-type criterion also met. Sales-type lease Day 1 journal entry: Dr. Net Investment in Lease (PV of lease payments = $520,782) / Cr. Equipment $500,000 / Cr. Selling Profit $20,782. The lessor derecognizes the asset from the balance sheet and recognizes a net investment receivable representing the PV of future lease payments. The $20,782 selling profit arises because the present value of what the lessor will receive ($520,782) exceeds its cost ($500,000). Over the lease term, the lessor recognizes interest income by applying the implicit rate to the net investment balance.

questions.name: Technical Accounting and Reporting
questions.keyword: Public company reporting — Regulation S-X/S-K requirements, XBRL business reporting (purpose and characteristics), operating segment identification criteria, reportable segment thresholds, segment note disclosure requirements
questions.text: Under ASC 280, an operating segment is reportable if it meets at least one of three quantitative thresholds. Which set of thresholds correctly identifies when a segment must be separately reported?

answers.text: The segment's revenues are at least 10% of combined revenues; or absolute amount of profit/loss is at least 10% of the greater of combined reported profit or combined reported loss; or assets are at least 10% of combined assets of all operating segments
The segment's revenues are at least 5% of combined revenues of all segments; or assets are at least 5% of combined assets
The segment has positive operating income — any segment with operating income must be separately disclosed
The segment's revenues are at least 15% of total consolidated revenues as reported in the income statement

explanations.a: ASC 280-10-50-12 specifies three quantitative thresholds for reportable segment determination — a segment is reportable if it meets ANY ONE: (1) Revenue threshold: reported revenues (including intersegment revenues) are 10% or more of the combined revenues of all operating segments; (2) Profit/loss threshold: absolute amount of reported profit/loss is 10% or more of the greater of: (a) combined reported profit of all operating segments that reported a profit, OR (b) combined reported loss of all operating segments that reported a loss; (3) Asset threshold: assets are 10% or more of the combined assets of all operating segments. Additionally, the aggregated revenues of all reportable segments must be at least 75% of consolidated revenues — if they are less, additional segments must be reported until the 75% threshold is met. A maximum of approximately 10 segments is considered practical.
explanations.b: The threshold is 10%, not 5%. Using 5% would require more segment disclosures than required under ASC 280, potentially fragmenting segment reporting beyond what is useful for investors.
explanations.c: Profitability alone does not determine reportability. A segment can be unprofitable (loss-generating) and still be reportable if it meets the size thresholds. The profit/loss threshold uses the absolute value (magnitude) of profit or loss, not its sign.
explanations.d: 15% is not a threshold in ASC 280. The correct threshold is 10%. Also, the threshold compares to combined segment revenues, not to total consolidated revenues (which may differ due to eliminations).

questions.name: Technical Accounting and Reporting
questions.keyword: Public company reporting — Regulation S-X/S-K requirements, XBRL business reporting (purpose and characteristics), operating segment identification criteria, reportable segment thresholds, segment note disclosure requirements
questions.text: A public company has five operating segments with the following data: Segment A revenues $400M, assets $300M; Segment B revenues $200M, assets $250M; Segment C revenues $80M, assets $100M; Segment D revenues $40M, assets $50M; Segment E revenues $30M, assets $40M. Total combined revenues = $750M; total combined assets = $740M. No segment has an operating loss. Determine which segments meet the 10% thresholds and must be reported separately.

answers.text: Only Segment A meets all thresholds and must be reported separately; all other segments are combined as 'Other'

Segments A, B, and C are reportable (each meets the revenue or asset threshold); Segments D and E are below thresholds and combined in 'Other'; the three reportable segments cover $680M/$750M = 90.7% of revenues, satisfying the 75% coverage test
Segments A and B are reportable; the combined revenues of A+B = $600M/$750M = 80%, satisfying the 75% test; C, D, and E are combined as 'Other'
All five segments must be reported separately because the 75% revenue coverage test requires that at least 75% of revenues be covered by reportable segments

explanations.a: Only reporting Segment A would cover $400M/$750M = 53% of revenues, falling well short of the required 75% coverage. More segments must be reported.
explanations.b: Threshold analysis: Revenue threshold (10% × $750M = $75M): Segment A: $400M ✓; Segment B: $200M ✓; Segment C: $80M ✓; Segment D: $40M ✗; Segment E: $30M ✗. Asset threshold (10% × $740M = $74M): Segment A: $300M ✓; Segment B: $250M ✓; Segment C: $100M ✓; Segment D: $50M ✗; Segment E: $40M ✗. Segments A, B, and C meet at least one threshold → reportable. D and E do not meet any threshold → combined in 'All Other.' 75% coverage test: Reportable segment revenues = $400M + $200M + $80M = $680M / $750M = 90.7% > 75% → sufficient. No additional segments need to be forced into separate reporting. D and E ($70M combined) are disclosed as 'All Other' with a reconciliation to consolidated totals.
explanations.c: Segments A and B cover $600M/$750M = 80% > 75%, so the 75% minimum is satisfied with just A and B. However, Segment C ($80M) also meets the 10% revenue threshold ($80M > $75M), so it must independently be reported — even though the 75% minimum would be satisfied without it. The 75% rule requires ADDITIONAL disclosure when thresholds fall short; it does not permit excluding segments that independently meet the 10% thresholds.
explanations.d: Not all five segments are required. The 75% coverage test is met with three reportable segments (90.7% > 75%). The 75% test only requires additional reporting when the reportable segments collectively cover less than 75% — not in this case.

questions.text: Under SEC rules, which regulation governs the form and content of financial statements included in SEC filings (such as Form 10-K and Form 10-Q), and what is the primary purpose of XBRL tagging requirements for public companies?

answers.text: Regulation S-K governs financial statement form and content; XBRL tagging is optional for large accelerated filers
Financial statement form and content is governed by GAAP only; SEC regulations apply only to non-financial disclosures

Regulation S-X governs the form and content of financial statements; XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language) tagging makes financial data machine-readable and structured, enabling automated data extraction, analysis, and comparison by investors, analysts, and regulators
Regulation S-K governs both financial statement form and XBRL requirements; S-X governs management discussion and analysis

explanations.a: Regulation S-K governs non-financial statement disclosures in SEC filings — business description, risk factors, legal proceedings, selected financial data, MD&A, and compensation disclosures. Regulation S-X (not S-K) governs financial statement form and content. XBRL is mandatory, not optional, for accelerated and large accelerated filers.
explanations.b: SEC regulations extensively govern how financial statements are presented in SEC filings — including required periods, auditor requirements, and industry-specific rules. GAAP alone (FASB standards) governs measurement and recognition; S-X governs presentation and disclosure in SEC filings, adding requirements beyond GAAP.
explanations.c: Regulatory framework for SEC filings: Regulation S-X: specifies the form, content, and auditing requirements of financial statements included in SEC filings. It covers: which periods must be presented (3 years of income statements, 2 years of balance sheets); the form of the audit report; specific rules for certain industries; financial statements for acquired businesses. Regulation S-K: specifies disclosure requirements for the non-financial portions of SEC filings including: MD&A (Management Discussion and Analysis); business description (Item 1); risk factors (Item 1A); executive compensation (Item 402); governance disclosures. XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language): the SEC requires public companies to tag financial statement data using XBRL (now iXBRL — Inline XBRL). Purpose: (1) Makes financial data structured and machine-readable; (2) Enables automated extraction and comparison across companies without manual re-keying; (3) Powers EDGAR's financial data search capabilities; (4) Improves accuracy by requiring companies to explicitly identify each financial data element using standard taxonomy tags.
explanations.d: Regulation S-K governs non-financial disclosures; Regulation S-X governs financial statement form. MD&A is an S-K requirement — it is a non-financial narrative, not a formal financial statement.

questions.text: A diversified conglomerate has three reportable segments: Technology, Manufacturing, and Retail. The Technology segment operates through multiple product lines — smartphones, tablets, and cloud services — that are managed separately. Management is considering aggregating these into one Technology segment. What criteria must be met for aggregation to be permissible under ASC 280?

answers.text: Aggregation is permissible whenever segments share the same industry classification code — SIC codes determine whether segments can be combined
Aggregation is permissible only if the segments are identical in all respects — any difference in product type, customer, or geography precludes aggregation
Aggregation is always permissible when the CODM reviews the segments together — management's internal review structure completely determines whether segments can be aggregated

Aggregation is permissible if the operating segments have similar economic characteristics AND are similar in: nature of products and services, nature of production processes, type/class of customer, distribution methods, and regulatory environment — all five qualitative criteria must be considered along with economic similarity

explanations.a: Industry classification codes (SIC or NAICS) are not the criterion for segment aggregation under ASC 280. The aggregation criteria focus on economic characteristics and qualitative similarities, not regulatory industry codes.
explanations.b: ASC 280 does not require identical characteristics for aggregation — it requires SIMILAR characteristics. Perfect identity would be so restrictive that essentially no aggregation would be permissible. The standard provides for judgment about whether similarities are sufficient.
explanations.c: The CODM's review structure determines whether a component IS an operating segment — but management's choice to review segments together does not alone permit aggregation. The economic similarity and qualitative criteria must also be met. Allowing pure management discretion in aggregation would undermine the disclosure objectives of ASC 280.
explanations.d: ASC 280-10-50-11 aggregation criteria: two or more operating segments may be aggregated into a single reportable segment if aggregation is consistent with the objective and principles of ASC 280, the segments have SIMILAR ECONOMIC CHARACTERISTICS (e.g., similar long-term average gross margins), AND the segments are similar in ALL of the following: (1) Nature of the products and services; (2) Nature of the production processes; (3) Type or class of customer for products and services; (4) Methods used to distribute products or provide services; (5) Nature of the regulatory environment, if applicable. For the Technology segment: Smartphones, tablets, and cloud services may have dissimilar production processes (hardware manufacturing vs. software/hosting), different distribution methods, and potentially different customer types (consumer vs. enterprise for cloud). These differences would need to be evaluated carefully — the three product lines may NOT qualify for aggregation if their economic characteristics or qualitative factors differ meaningfully.

questions.text: Which financial statements are required for a defined benefit pension plan under ASC 960?

answers.text: Statement of net assets available for benefits (as of the plan year-end) and statement of changes in net assets available for benefits (for the plan year)
Income statement, balance sheet, statement of cash flows, and statement of stockholders' equity — the same as a regular corporate entity
Statement of plan net position and statement of changes in plan net position — the same terminology as governmental accounting
Only a statement of funded status comparing plan assets to the projected benefit obligation — no other financial statements are required

explanations.a: Under ASC 960 (Defined Benefit Pension Plans) and ASC 962 (Defined Contribution Plans), the primary financial statements for pension plans filed annually with the DOL (Department of Labor) on Form 5500 are: (1) Statement of Net Assets Available for Benefits: presents the plan's assets (investments, receivables, property) minus liabilities (benefits payable, administrative expenses payable) = net assets available for benefits. This is the plan's 'balance sheet' as of year-end; (2) Statement of Changes in Net Assets Available for Benefits: presents additions to and deductions from net assets during the year. Additions: employer contributions, employee contributions, investment income, net realized/unrealized gains. Deductions: benefit payments to participants, administrative expenses. Net change = ending net assets minus beginning net assets.
explanations.b: Employee benefit plans (pension plans, 401(k) plans) do not prepare the same financial statements as operating corporations. They are not-for-profit entities with specialized reporting objectives — reporting the plan's assets available to pay future benefits and how those assets changed during the year.
explanations.c: 'Statement of plan net position' and 'statement of changes in plan net position' are GASB terms used for governmental pension plans (GASB 67/68). The FASB ASC terms for private-sector pension plans are 'statement of net assets available for benefits' and 'statement of changes in net assets available for benefits.'
explanations.d: A statement of funded status (comparing plan assets to the PBO) appears in the PLAN SPONSOR's financial statements (the employer company's GAAP financials) under ASC 715, not in the plan's own financial statements. The plan entity itself files the two statements described in option B.

questions.text: A defined benefit pension plan has the following information for the current year: beginning net assets available for benefits $4,500,000; employer contributions $600,000; employee contributions $200,000; investment income (realized and unrealized gains, dividends) $350,000; benefit payments to retirees $480,000; administrative expenses $45,000. Prepare the statement of changes in net assets available for benefits and determine the ending net assets.

answers.text: Ending net assets = $5,125,000; additions = $1,150,000; deductions = $525,000

Ending net assets = $5,125,000 — statement format: Additions: employer contributions $600,000 + employee contributions $200,000 + investment income $350,000 = $1,150,000; Deductions: benefits paid $480,000 + admin expenses $45,000 = $525,000; Net increase = $625,000; Beginning net assets $4,500,000 + $625,000 = $5,125,000
Ending net assets = $4,625,000; total additions = $1,150,000; total deductions = $525,000; net change = $625,000; $4,500,000 + $625,000 = $5,125,000
Ending net assets = $4,870,000 — only employer contributions and benefit payments affect the statement; employee contributions and investment income are not included in plan financial statements

explanations.a: The ending net assets figure ($5,125,000) is correct and this option correctly states additions and deductions, but option C provides the fully formatted statement layout.
explanations.b: Statement of Changes in Net Assets Available for Benefits: Additions: Employer contributions: $600,000; Employee contributions: $200,000; Investment income (net realized/unrealized gains + dividends + interest): $350,000; Total additions: $1,150,000. Deductions: Benefits paid to participants and beneficiaries: $480,000; Administrative expenses: $45,000; Total deductions: $525,000. Net increase in net assets: $1,150,000 − $525,000 = $625,000. Net assets available for benefits, beginning of year: $4,500,000. Net assets available for benefits, end of year: $5,125,000. The statement format differs from a corporate income statement — there is no 'net income' or 'profit' concept; the measure is changes in net assets available to pay future retirement benefits.
explanations.c: This option has a mathematical error — it states ending net assets = $4,625,000 but then adds $4,500,000 + $625,000 = $5,125,000 in the same answer. The correct ending balance is $5,125,000.
explanations.d: Employee contributions and investment income are both included in the plan's statement of changes in net assets. Employee contributions represent participants adding to their benefit accruals; investment income is how the plan grows its assets to meet future obligations. Both are core additions in the plan's financial statements.

questions.text: A company sponsors a defined benefit pension plan. The plan sponsor's (employer's) financial statements must reflect the funded status under ASC 715. The PBO is $8,000,000, the fair value of plan assets is $6,500,000, and the accumulated OCI (prior service cost) is $400,000. How does the plan sponsor recognize these amounts on its balance sheet and in OCI?

answers.text: The company records only cash contributions made to the plan — ASC 715 does not require balance sheet recognition of pension obligations
The company records only the net periodic pension cost as an expense — the funded status appears only in the notes to financial statements, not on the balance sheet

The company records a pension liability of $1,500,000 (PBO minus plan assets); additionally, the unrecognized prior service cost of $400,000 is recorded in AOCI and amortized to pension expense over the employees' remaining service period
The full PBO of $8,000,000 is recorded as a liability and the plan assets of $6,500,000 are recorded as an asset, each disclosed separately on the balance sheet

explanations.a: ASC 715 (issued in 2006) specifically requires full recognition of the funded status on the balance sheet — the net underfunded or overfunded amount appears as a liability or asset. This was a major change from prior pension accounting that allowed off-balance-sheet deferral.
explanations.b: ASC 715 explicitly requires balance sheet recognition of the net funded status, not just note disclosure. The full underfunded or overfunded position appears on the face of the balance sheet. This was the key innovation of ASC 715 — bringing pension obligations onto the balance sheet.
explanations.c: ASC 715 balance sheet recognition: Funded status = Plan assets FV ($6,500,000) − PBO ($8,000,000) = −$1,500,000 (underfunded). The company records: Dr. Other Comprehensive Income — Prior Service Cost $400,000 (if not yet recognized); Cr. Pension Liability $1,500,000; Dr. Pension Asset/AOCI (net). Net balance sheet impact: Pension liability of $1,500,000 (net underfunded amount). The prior service cost ($400,000) represents the cost of benefit improvements granted to employees for prior service — it is recognized in OCI at the plan amendment date and amortized to pension expense over the average remaining service period of affected employees using the straight-line method or corridor approach. The AOCI balance represents costs that have been recognized in comprehensive income but not yet 'recycled' through net income.
explanations.d: While the gross amounts (PBO and plan assets) are disclosed in the notes, the balance sheet itself presents only the NET funded status (plan assets minus PBO = −$1,500,000 liability). Gross presentation of both PBO and assets separately on the balance sheet is not GAAP.

questions.text: A company's defined benefit pension plan has the following Year 2 activity: service cost $300,000; interest cost $400,000; expected return on plan assets −$350,000; amortization of prior service cost $50,000; amortization of net actuarial loss $75,000; settlement loss $0. Calculate net periodic pension cost for Year 2, and explain where each component is recognized in the financial statements under ASC 715-30.

answers.text: Net periodic pension cost = $475,000; all components are reported in operating income as a single line item
Net periodic pension cost = $700,000; all components except expected return are recognized in operating income
Net periodic pension cost = $475,000; all components are recognized in OCI and amortized to income over the plan participants' service periods

Net periodic pension cost = $475,000; under ASC 715-20 (updated ASC 2017-07), service cost is recognized in operating income; all other components (interest cost, expected return, amortization of PSC and actuarial losses) are recognized in non-operating income/expense (below operating income) or as a separate line item

explanations.a: Under ASU 2017-07, the presentation of net periodic pension cost is NOT all in operating income. Service cost must be presented in operating income (or wherever compensation costs are reported), while all other components must be presented outside of operations. Presenting all components as a single operating income line violates ASU 2017-07.
explanations.b: Service cost only (not all components except expected return) is presented in operating income. Additionally, $700,000 = $300,000 + $400,000 − $0 + $0 + $0 would ignore the expected return and amortization components. The correct total is $475,000.
explanations.c: OCI treatment applies to the recognition of changes in actuarial assumptions, plan amendments (prior service cost), and the difference between expected and actual return — these go to OCI initially and are AMORTIZED from OCI to net periodic pension cost. The periodic pension cost itself (already the amortized OCI amounts) flows through income, not OCI.
explanations.d: Net periodic pension cost calculation: Service cost: $300,000. Interest cost: $400,000. Expected return on plan assets: −$350,000. Amortization of prior service cost: $50,000. Amortization of net actuarial loss: $75,000. Net periodic pension cost = $300,000 + $400,000 − $350,000 + $50,000 + $75,000 = $475,000. Presentation under ASU 2017-07 (effective 2018): (1) Service cost ($300,000): presented in operating income in the same line as or adjacent to other employee compensation costs — the only pension component that can be in operating income; (2) All other components — interest cost, expected return, amortization of PSC, amortization of actuarial gains/losses — must be presented OUTSIDE of operating income (typically as 'non-operating income/expense' or in a separate section below operating income). This presentation change was designed to improve transparency by separating the employment-service-related pension cost from the financing/investment components.

questions.text: Under ASC 321, how are investments in equity securities (other than those accounted for under the equity method or consolidated) measured subsequent to acquisition?

answers.text: At fair value, with unrealized holding gains and losses reported in net income
At cost, with no subsequent remeasurement unless there is a permanent decline in value
At fair value, with unrealized holding gains and losses reported in other comprehensive income (OCI)
At the lower of cost or market, with write-downs to market recognized in income and subsequent recoveries prohibited

explanations.a: Under ASC 321-10-35-1, equity securities with readily determinable fair values are measured at fair value, with ALL changes in fair value (both realized and unrealized gains and losses) recognized in net income each period. This was a fundamental change from prior guidance — equity securities are no longer classified as AFS (with OCI treatment). The change means that holding large equity portfolios creates income statement volatility, as unrealized market fluctuations immediately affect reported earnings.
explanations.b: The cost method was permitted under pre-2016 guidance for equity securities without readily determinable fair values. ASC 321 (effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017) changed this — most equity securities are now measured at fair value, not cost. Limited exceptions apply for equity securities without readily determinable fair values (which may use the measurement alternative — cost minus impairment plus observable price changes).
explanations.c: This was the treatment for AVAILABLE-FOR-SALE equity securities under the old ASC 320 framework (pre-2016). ASU 2016-01 eliminated the AFS category for equity securities — unrealized gains and losses on equity securities can no longer be deferred in OCI. Under ASC 321, changes in fair value go directly to net income.
explanations.d: Lower of cost or market was an inventory accounting concept. It was not a standard measurement basis for long-term equity investments, even under prior guidance. Under ASC 321, fair value (through income) is the required measurement basis.

questions.text: A company purchases corporate bonds for $500,000 and classifies them as available-for-sale (AFS). At year-end, the bonds' fair value has declined to $460,000. Management determines that $25,000 of the $40,000 decline is attributable to credit losses (risk of default), and $15,000 is attributable to non-credit factors (rising interest rates). Under ASU 2016-13 (CECL), how is this decline recorded?

answers.text: The entire $40,000 decline is recognized as a credit loss in net income — all fair value declines on AFS debt securities are impairment losses

The $25,000 credit loss component is recognized in net income through an allowance for credit losses; the $15,000 non-credit decline remains in OCI as an unrealized loss — the credit portion flows through income, the non-credit portion stays in OCI
No impairment is recorded — AFS securities can only be impaired if the company intends to sell or is more likely than not to be required to sell
The entire $40,000 is recorded in OCI as an unrealized loss — AFS securities always use OCI for all fair value changes

explanations.a: Under ASU 2016-13 (CECL, effective for SEC filers for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2019), AFS debt security impairment is split between credit-related and non-credit-related components. Recording the entire decline in income would overstate credit impairment losses and remove the non-credit portion from OCI.
explanations.b: ASU 2016-13 AFS debt security impairment: When an AFS debt security's fair value falls below amortized cost, the entity: (1) Determines whether the decline is credit-related or non-credit-related; (2) Credit loss portion ($25,000): recognized in net income through an 'allowance for credit losses' (a contra-asset to the security). Journal entry: Dr. Credit Loss Expense $25,000 / Cr. Allowance for Credit Losses $25,000; (3) Non-credit portion ($15,000): remains in OCI as an unrealized loss (the security still reported at FV = $460,000, with carrying value of $500,000 − $25,000 allowance = $475,000, and the remaining $15,000 decline in OCI). Journal entry: Dr. OCI — Unrealized Loss $15,000 / Cr. AFS Security (or AOCI) $15,000. If interest rates later decline and the non-credit loss reverses, the OCI recovery is recognized; if the credit loss improves, the allowance can be reversed through income.
explanations.c: The intent/ability to sell test is still relevant — if the company INTENDS to sell the security or is MORE LIKELY THAN NOT to be required to sell before recovery, then the entire fair value decline (not just the credit portion) is recognized in income. However, if the company does not intend to sell and is not required to sell, the CECL approach separates credit and non-credit portions.
explanations.d: Under pre-CECL guidance, the entire AFS unrealized change went to OCI unless deemed 'other-than-temporary impairment' (OTTI). Under ASU 2016-13, credit-related impairment goes to income through an allowance — OCI only captures non-credit fair value changes.

questions.text: A company holds the following investments: (1) IBM common stock purchased on NYSE; (2) A corporate bond whose fair value is estimated using a discounted cash flow model with company-specific credit spread assumptions not observable in the market; (3) A U.S. Treasury note actively traded with observable quoted prices. Classify each investment's fair value measurement in the ASC 820 fair value hierarchy.

answers.text: All three are Level 1 — publicly traded securities always qualify for Level 1 regardless of pricing methodology
IBM stock: Level 2; Treasury note: Level 1; Corporate bond: Level 2 — corporate bonds are always Level 2 because they trade in less active markets than equities
IBM stock: Level 1; Treasury note: Level 1; Corporate bond: Level 3 — the company's own credit spread assumptions are unobservable
Treasury note: Level 1; IBM stock: Level 1; Corporate bond: Level 2 — corporate bond fair value uses observable yield curves even if company-specific spreads are estimated

explanations.a: The level depends on the INPUTS used in the fair value measurement, not simply whether the security is publicly traded. Corporate bonds may trade publicly but if their fair value is estimated using unobservable company-specific inputs, they are Level 3.
explanations.b: IBM stock on NYSE is Level 1 (active market, identical asset, unadjusted price) — not Level 2. Corporate bonds using unobservable company-specific inputs are Level 3, not Level 2. Level 2 would apply to a corporate bond priced using observable market yields and credit spreads from similar companies.
explanations.c: Fair value hierarchy classification: (1) IBM common stock (NYSE): Level 1 — unadjusted quoted price in an active market for an identical asset (closing price on NYSE). Level 1 is the most observable and reliable; (2) U.S. Treasury note (actively traded, observable prices): Level 1 — quoted prices in active markets for identical securities. Treasury securities trade in highly liquid, active markets with transparent prices; (3) Corporate bond (DCF model with company-specific credit spreads not observable in the market): Level 3 — the use of UNOBSERVABLE inputs (company-specific credit spread assumptions) makes this a Level 3 measurement, even if the DCF model itself is standard. The key is whether the inputs are observable in the market — company-specific assumptions that cannot be corroborated by market data push the measurement to Level 3. This is significant for financial statement disclosure purposes: Level 3 requires the most extensive disclosures, including a rollforward of the Level 3 balance and sensitivity analysis.
explanations.d: If the corporate bond's fair value uses UNOBSERVABLE company-specific credit spread assumptions (as stated in the question), it is Level 3 — not Level 2. Observable yield curves would make it Level 2, but the question specifies the spreads are 'not observable in the market.'

questions.text: A company classifies a portfolio of municipal bonds as held-to-maturity (HTM). At year-end, management calculates that $80,000 of expected credit losses exist on the portfolio over the remaining contractual term using the CECL model. The portfolio's amortized cost is $2,000,000 and fair value is $1,900,000. Analyze the accounting impact and the constraint on reclassifying HTM securities.

answers.text: The company records a $100,000 unrealized loss in OCI — HTM securities are measured at fair value like AFS securities
The company must reclassify to AFS because the fair value decline of $100,000 triggers mandatory reclassification
No accounting entry is required — HTM securities are only adjusted when sold or matured, not for credit losses

The company records an $80,000 allowance for credit losses under CECL; the securities remain at amortized cost minus the $80,000 allowance = $1,920,000; the $100,000 fair value decline below amortized cost is NOT recorded because HTM securities are not remeasured to fair value; selling HTM securities taints the entire HTM portfolio

explanations.a: HTM securities are carried at AMORTIZED COST, not fair value. The fair value of $1,900,000 is disclosed in the notes but is NOT used to adjust the carrying amount on the balance sheet. OCI is used for AFS securities — not HTM. The $100,000 fair value decline below amortized cost does not trigger any accounting recognition under the HTM model (outside of credit losses).
explanations.b: Fair value declines below amortized cost do not trigger mandatory reclassification out of HTM. Only credit impairment (expected credit losses) is recognized under CECL. A company may elect to reclassify (which would taint the portfolio) but is not required to do so solely because of fair value declines.
explanations.c: CECL requires HTM entities to estimate and recognize expected credit losses using an allowance model — even before any actual defaults occur. Simply waiting for sale or maturity ignores the CECL requirement for proactive credit loss recognition.
explanations.d: HTM security accounting under ASU 2016-13 (CECL) and ASC 320: (1) HTM securities are carried at amortized cost on the balance sheet — the $1,900,000 fair value is not the carrying amount. Carrying amount = amortized cost $2,000,000; (2) CECL requires HTM entities to recognize expected credit losses using an allowance: Dr. Credit Loss Expense $80,000 / Cr. Allowance for Credit Losses — HTM $80,000. Carrying amount net of allowance = $2,000,000 − $80,000 = $1,920,000; (3) Fair value decline ($100,000) not recognized: the additional $20,000 ($100,000 fair value decline − $80,000 credit loss) represents non-credit factors (interest rate risk) that are not recognized for HTM securities — this is by design, as the company intends to hold to maturity and will recover the amortized cost unless there are credit defaults; (4) Tainting rule: if the company sells or transfers a significant amount of HTM securities before maturity (except in limited circumstances such as within 3 months of maturity, or due to deterioration in creditworthiness), the entire HTM portfolio becomes 'tainted' and must be reclassified to AFS — undermining the held-to-maturity assertion. This creates a strong discipline against selling HTM securities before maturity.
